lead: Distillation separates liquid mixtures by boiling point using repeated vapour-liquid equilibrium stages. This unit moves from equilibrium and simple batch stills to McCabe-Thiele and Ponchon-Savarit design, reflux choice, column hardware and multicomponent shortcuts. After it you can size a binary column, read an enthalpy-composition diagram, and choose a method for azeotrope problems.
about: The unit starts with 4.1, vapour-liquid equilibrium and Raoult's law, because every distillation calculation needs the y-x relation. 4.2 and 4.3 apply that relation to flash, simple, differential and steam distillation. 4.4 builds the McCabe-Thiele stage construction, and 4.5 explains how reflux ratio sets stage count and cost. 4.6 repeats the design on an enthalpy-composition diagram with Ponchon-Savarit. 4.7 turns theoretical stages into real trays or packing through efficiency. 4.8 gives the Fenske, Underwood and Gilliland shortcuts for multicomponent mixtures. 4.9 closes with azeotropic and extractive distillation, where a solvent or entrainer defeats an azeotrope.

chapters.idea: At equilibrium the vapour and liquid compositions of an ideal binary mixture are fixed by component vapour pressures and total pressure.
chapters.depth: Define mole fraction x in liquid and y in vapour, total pressure P, pure-component vapour pressures P°A and P°B. Derive Raoult's law p_A = x_A P°A and Dalton's law P = p_A + p_B. Show the bubble-point equation x_A = (P - P°B)/(P°A - P°B) and y_A = x_A P°A/P. Define relative volatility α = (y_A/x_A)/(y_B/x_B) = P°A/P°B for ideal Raoult's law. Draw y-x and T-x-y diagrams; note non-ideal systems and azeotrope as α = 1. Some syllabi call this vapour-liquid equilibrium (VLE). Keep activity coefficients as a mention only.

figure.aria: Equilibrium y-x curve for relative volatility 3, lying above the diagonal y = x.
figure.caption: equilibrium curve for α = 3; it lies above the diagonal

chapters.example: A binary ideal mixture has P°A = 120 kPa and P°B = 40 kPa at the column pressure P = 101.3 kPa. Find the equilibrium liquid and vapour mole fractions of A. Solution: x_A = (101.3 - 40)/(120 - 40) = 61.3/80 = 0.766. y_A = x_A P°A/P = 0.766 × 120/101.3 = 0.908. Relative volatility α = 120/40 = 3.0.
chapters.trap: Mixing up x and y; Raoult's law gives partial pressure from liquid x, not from vapour y. Also α = 1 at an azeotrope, not a constant for real systems.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 diffusion ideas are not needed; basic mole fraction and Dalton's law from chemistry are enough.
chapters.leave: Activity-coefficient models and non-ideal VLE prediction are left to thermodynamics; stage efficiency is in 4.7.

chapters.idea: Flash distillation separates a feed in one equilibrium stage by partially vaporising it and removing vapour and liquid separately.
chapters.depth: Define feed F (kmol/h), feed mole fraction z, vapour V, liquid L, vapour fraction V/F. Write component balance F z = V y + L x and equilibrium y = K x. Define K value. Derive Rachford-Rice equation Σ z_i (K_i - 1)/(1 + (V/F)(K_i - 1)) = 0 for multicomponent flash; show binary solution. Explain flash drum with heater, pressure reduction and knockout. Include isothermal and adiabatic flash as names. Some syllabi call this equilibrium vaporization.

figure.aria: Block diagram of a flash drum: feed is heated, then separated into vapour and liquid.
figure.caption: one equilibrium stage: heat the feed, then split vapour and liquid in the flash drum

chapters.example: A flash drum receives F = 100 kmol/h of a binary feed with z_A = 0.50 at a pressure where K_A = 2.0 and K_B = 0.5. The vapour fraction is V/F = 0.50. Find V, L, x_A and y_A. Check Rachford-Rice: 0.5(2-1)/(1+0.5(2-1)) + 0.5(0.5-1)/(1+0.5(0.5-1)) = 0.333 - 0.333 = 0. Then x_A = z_A/[1 + (V/F)(K_A - 1)] = 0.50/[1+0.5(1)] = 0.333. y_A = K_A x_A = 0.667. V = 50 kmol/h, L = 50 kmol/h.
chapters.trap: Using x = z directly; the feed composition z is not the liquid composition after flash. Also K depends on T and P; do not treat K as a fixed constant outside the stated condition.
chapters.leave: Multicomponent Rachford-Rice numerical solution is in 4.8; condenser and reboiler details in 4.4.

chapters.idea: Simple distillation removes vapour as it forms and gives a Rayleigh equation; steam distillation lowers the boiling temperature by adding immiscible steam.
chapters.depth: Derive Rayleigh equation ln(L1/L2) = ∫_{x2}^{x1} dx/(y - x) for a batch still with no reflux. For constant α show the integrated form. Define L1 initial charge, L2 final residue, x1 and x2 liquid mole fractions, D distillate. Explain differential distillation as another name. For steam distillation: immiscible water and organic, total pressure P = p_water° + p_organic°, so boiling occurs below the normal boiling point of each; use steam to strip a heat-sensitive organic. Keep steam consumption as a simple mention. Batch distillation with reflux is only named.

figure.aria: Batch still block diagram: charge enters the still pot, vapour is condensed as distillate, and residue remains; steam can be added for steam distillation.
figure.caption: batch still: vapour is condensed as distillate while the residue becomes richer in the less volatile component

chapters.example: A batch still charges L1 = 100 mol of an ideal binary liquid with x1 = 0.50 and constant α = 2.0. Distillation stops when the residue liquid reaches x2 = 0.20. Use Rayleigh equation for constant α: ln(L1/L2) = [ln(x1/x2) - α ln((1 - x1)/(1 - x2))]/(α - 1). Substitute: ln(0.50/0.20) = 0.916; ln((0.50)/(0.80)) = -0.470; numerator = 0.916 - 2(-0.470) = 1.856; divide by 1 = 1.856. L1/L2 = e^1.856 = 6.40. L2 = 100/6.40 = 15.6 mol. Distillate D = 100 - 15.6 = 84.4 mol.
chapters.trap: Using the equilibrium y in place of the changing distillate composition; Rayleigh equation needs y in equilibrium with the liquid x at each moment. Also steam distillation needs immiscible liquids, not a soluble solvent.
chapters.leave: Batch distillation with reflux and multiple fractions is not derived here; see a batch column in 4.7.

chapters.idea: McCabe-Thiele finds the number of theoretical stages by stepping between the equilibrium curve and the operating lines on a y-x diagram.
chapters.depth: Define rectifying section, stripping section, feed line (q-line), q = fraction of feed that is liquid. Write rectifying operating line y = (R/(R+1))x + x_D/(R+1); stripping line through (x_B,x_B) and the feed intersection. Define R = L/D reflux ratio. Explain the steps: start at (x_D,x_D), horizontal to equilibrium, vertical to operating line, repeat to x_B; count stages including reboiler. Use constant α equilibrium curve. Show feed line for saturated liquid (q=1, vertical), saturated vapour (q=0, horizontal) and two-phase. Some syllabi spell it McCabe and Thiele.

figure.aria: McCabe-Thiele construction on a y-x plot: equilibrium curve, rectifying line, stripping line and vertical q-line at x=0.4.
figure.caption: construction lines for x_D=0.95, x_B=0.05, x_F=0.40 and R=2; the q-line is at x_F

chapters.example: A binary column has α = 2.5, saturated-liquid feed with x_F = 0.40, distillate x_D = 0.95 and bottoms x_B = 0.05. Reflux ratio R = 2.0. Find the rectifying and stripping operating lines and the theoretical stages. Rectifying line: y = (2/3)x + 0.95/3 = 0.667x + 0.317. Equilibrium vapour at x_F: y_F* = 2.5(0.40)/(1 + 1.5(0.40)) = 0.625. Feed point is (0.40, 0.583) from the rectifying line. Stripping line through (0.05,0.05) and (0.40,0.583): slope = (0.583 - 0.05)/(0.40 - 0.05) = 1.524; y = 1.524x - 0.026. Stepping gives about 13 equilibrium stages including the reboiler.
chapters.trap: Stepping to the operating line instead of the equilibrium curve, or counting the reboiler twice. The q-line is not an operating line; it locates the feed intersection.
chapters.leave: Minimum and optimum reflux in 4.5; enthalpy method in 4.6; real tray efficiency in 4.7.

chapters.idea: The reflux ratio sets the trade-off between stage count and operating cost: minimum reflux needs infinite stages, total reflux needs minimum stages, and the optimum is near minimum cost.
chapters.depth: Define R = L/D. At minimum reflux R_min an operating line touches the equilibrium curve at the pinch; for saturated-liquid feed R_min = (x_D - y_F*)/(y_F* - x_F). At total reflux R → ∞, operating lines coincide with the diagonal and Fenske gives N_min = log[(x_D/(1-x_D))((1-x_B)/x_B)]/log α. Optimum reflux is usually 1.2 to 1.5 R_min, where total annual cost is lowest. Only a few universities teach this topic in detail.

figure.aria: Illustrative cost curve against reflux ratio, with a minimum marked near R=1.88.
figure.caption: total cost falls then rises; the lowest point is near 1.3 to 1.5 times R_min

chapters.example: For α = 2.5, x_F = 0.40 saturated liquid, x_D = 0.95, x_B = 0.05: equilibrium vapour at x_F is y_F* = 0.625. R_min = (0.95 - 0.625)/(0.625 - 0.40) = 1.44. If the chosen optimum is 1.3 R_min, R_opt = 1.3 × 1.44 = 1.88. Minimum stages by Fenske: N_min = log[(0.95/0.05)(0.95/0.05)]/log 2.5 = log(361)/log(2.5) = 6.4 stages.
chapters.trap: Using R_min as a working reflux; at R_min the required stages become infinite. Also Fenske gives stages at total reflux, not at the operating reflux.
chapters.leave: Economic cost data and detailed pinch analysis are outside this book.

chapters.idea: Ponchon-Savarit uses enthalpy-composition lines and difference points to design distillation without assuming constant molar overflow.
chapters.depth: Draw H-x and h-x curves for saturated vapour and liquid. Define difference point Δ_D for the rectifying section with abscissa x_D and ordinate H_ΔD = H_V + R(H_V - h_L) when H_V and h_L are constant. Operating lines are straight lines through Δ_D; equilibrium stages are found by stepping between the equilibrium tie line and the operating line. Define Δ_B for stripping. Show that McCabe-Thiele is the special case of equal latent heats. Keep construction qualitative; no full graphical stage count.

figure.aria: Enthalpy-composition plot with vapour and liquid lines and the rectifying difference point at x=0.95, enthalpy 110.
figure.caption: difference point for x_D=0.95, H_V=50 kJ/mol, h_L=20 kJ/mol and R=2 lies above the vapour line

chapters.example: A saturated-vapour enthalpy H_V = 50 kJ/mol and saturated-liquid enthalpy h_L = 20 kJ/mol are constant. The distillate is x_D = 0.95 and reflux ratio R = 2.0. Find the ordinate of the rectifying difference point Δ_D. H_ΔD = H_V + R(H_V - h_L) = 50 + 2(50 - 20) = 110 kJ/mol. The point is (0.95, 110) on the H-x diagram.
chapters.trap: Putting the difference point on the equilibrium curve; it is a fixed construction point, usually above the H-x curve. Forgetting that H and h are per mole of mixture, not per mole of one component.
chapters.prereq: 4.1 VLE; 4.4 operating lines; basic enthalpy balances from thermodynamics.
chapters.leave: Full graphical stage stepping with variable enthalpy is left to a worked tutorial; real tray efficiency is 4.7.

chapters.idea: Real columns use trays or packing; tray efficiency converts theoretical stages into actual trays by allowing for imperfect contact.
chapters.depth: Describe sieve, bubble-cap and valve trays; random and structured packing. Define overall tray efficiency E_o = N_theoretical/N_actual and Murphree vapour efficiency E_M = (y_n - y_{n+1})/(y_n* - y_{n+1}), where y_n* is vapour in equilibrium with liquid leaving tray n. Mention HETP for packed columns and that packed towers use HTU/NTU in Unit 3. Explain weeping, flooding and entrainment as limits. Some syllabi call E_o the column efficiency.

figure.aria: Block diagram of a tray column: condenser, rectifying trays, feed tray, stripping trays and reboiler.
figure.caption: a tray column has a rectifying section above the feed and a stripping section below; packing replaces the trays in a packed column

chapters.example: A column needs N_t = 10 theoretical stages. The overall tray efficiency is E_o = 0.60. Find the number of actual trays. N_actual = N_t/E_o = 10/0.60 = 16.7, so use 17 actual trays. On one tray the vapour entering from below has y_{n+1} = 0.30 and the equilibrium vapour with the leaving liquid is y_n* = 0.50. If the Murphree efficiency is E_M = 0.70, find the leaving vapour y_n. y_n = y_{n+1} + E_M(y_n* - y_{n+1}) = 0.30 + 0.70(0.50 - 0.30) = 0.44.
chapters.trap: Dividing by efficiency the wrong way: actual trays = theoretical/efficiency, so efficiency below 1 increases tray count. y_n* uses the liquid on the tray, not the incoming liquid.
chapters.prereq: 4.4 theoretical stages; Unit 3 packed tower HTU/NTU for packed columns.
chapters.leave: Packed tower design equations are in Unit 3; tray hydraulics and weeping/flooding correlations are not derived here.

chapters.idea: Multicomponent distillation uses shortcut methods: Fenske for minimum stages, Underwood for minimum reflux, Gilliland for the stage count at a chosen reflux.
chapters.depth: Define light key (LK) and heavy key (HK). Fenske: N_min = log[(d_LK/b_LK)(b_HK/d_HK)]/log α_LK-HK, with d and b distillate and bottoms flow rates. Underwood equations: solve Σ α_i z_i/(α_i - θ) = 1 - q for θ between key α values, then R_min + 1 = Σ α_i x_Di/(α_i - θ). Gilliland correlation uses X = (R - R_min)/(R + 1) and Y = (N - N_min)/(N + 1). Mention that the shortcuts assume constant α and constant molar overflow. Keep non-key distribution as a definition only.

figure.aria: Shortcut sequence block diagram: choose keys, Fenske for minimum stages, Underwood for minimum reflux, Gilliland for stages, then actual stages.
figure.caption: shortcut sequence: Fenske, then Underwood, then Gilliland

chapters.example: A binary key mixture has α_LK-HK = 2.0, x_D,LK = 0.98 and x_B,LK = 0.02. Find N_min by Fenske. N_min = log[(0.98/0.02)(0.98/0.02)]/log 2.0 = log(49 × 49)/0.301 = log(2401)/0.301 = 3.380/0.301 = 11.2 stages. For saturated-liquid feed with x_F = 0.50, equilibrium y_F* = 2(0.50)/(1 + 0.50) = 0.667. R_min = (0.98 - 0.667)/(0.667 - 0.50) = 0.313/0.167 = 1.88.
chapters.trap: Using the key relative volatility for all components; Fenske and Underwood use each component's α. Also N_min is at total reflux, not the design reflux.
chapters.leave: Rigorous multicomponent stage-by-stage calculation and tray efficiency are left to software; 4.7 covers efficiency.

chapters.idea: An azeotrope has equal vapour and liquid compositions, so ordinary distillation cannot cross it; azeotropic or extractive distillation adds a separating agent to shift the equilibrium.
chapters.depth: Define azeotrope: y_i = x_i and α = 1; minimum-boiling and maximum-boiling types. Explain azeotropic distillation with an entrainer that forms a new azeotrope, and extractive distillation with a high-boiling solvent fed near the top that changes relative volatility. Draw the two-column scheme with solvent recovery and recycle. Mention pressure-swing distillation as an alternative. Use ethanol-water as the standard example: about 95.6 mass % ethanol at 1 atm. Keep solvent selection qualitative.

figure.aria: Extractive distillation block diagram: feed enters the extractive column, overhead product leaves, solvent is recovered and recycled.
figure.caption: extractive distillation: solvent enters near the top and is recovered and recycled

chapters.example: An ethanol-water feed of 100 kg contains 50 mass % ethanol. At 1 atm the minimum-boiling azeotrope is about 95.6 mass % ethanol. Ordinary distillation from this water-rich feed can give pure water as bottoms and an overhead at the azeotrope. Find the maximum overhead mass if the overhead is at 95.6 mass % ethanol and the ethanol is taken overhead. Ethanol in feed = 0.50 × 100 = 50 kg. Overhead D = 50/0.956 = 52.3 kg. Bottoms = 100 - 52.3 = 47.7 kg, essentially water. Extractive distillation with a solvent is needed to get ethanol above 95.6 mass %.
chapters.trap: Thinking a longer column can cross an azeotrope; at α = 1 the stages do nothing. Also the entrainer in azeotropic distillation leaves with the overhead, while the solvent in extractive distillation leaves at the bottom and is recycled.
chapters.leave: Solvent screening and detailed ternary VLE are left to specialised texts; extraction is in Unit 5.
